sentences.text: Dracovenator was a medium-sized, ground-dwelling, bipedal carnivore estimated to reach 5.5 to 6.5 meters in length and 250 kilograms in mass.
This predator possessed a distinct kink in its upper jaws located between the maxilla and the premaxilla, a feature unique within its family due to the raised shape of its premaxilla.
The posterior end of Dracovenator's lower jaw features a variety of masses or protuberances.
Some estimates suggest Dracovenator was the largest member of the family Dilophosauridae, reaching 7 meters in length.
The species name D. regenti honors the late Regent "Lucas" Huma, who was a field assistant to Professor Kitching.

The genus name Dracovenator is a contraction of the Latin words for "dragon" and "hunter", meaning "dragon hunter" or "dragon catcher", with the name "Draco" referring to the discovery location in the Drakensberg foothills, meaning "Mountain of the Dragon".
Adam M. Yates described and named the type species Dracovenator regenti in 2005, with the formal description published in 2006.
The holotype of Dracovenator was found at the "Granja Drumbo Superior" locality in the Elliot Formation by James Kitching and Regent "Lucas" Huma.

The type material for Dracovenator was discovered at the Upper Drumbo Farm locality in the upper Elliot Formation in the Eastern Cape Province, South Africa, with the paratype specimen discovered by Munyikwa and Raath in 1999 and another paratype found in 1981.
Dracovenator is thought to have preyed on prosauropod dinosaurs within its paleoenvironment, and researchers believe Dracovenator fed on prosauropods in its paleoenvironment.
Yates assigned Dracovenator to the clade Neotheropoda in 2005 and classified Dracovenator within the family Dilophosauridae alongside the basal theropods Dilophosaurus and Zupaysaurus.
Cladistic analysis indicates that Dracovenator forms a clade with the basal theropods Dilophosaurus and Zupaysaurus.
Dracovenator lived from the Hettangian to the Sinemurian, between 201.4 and 192.9 million years ago.
Fossils of Dracovenator are housed at the Bernard Price Institute for Palaeontological Research in Johannesburg, South Africa.
